intro: After the child falls asleep, the poet has the last word. A G-major hymn breaks into hesitant piano speech, then gathers itself for the quietest of farewells.

sections.label: C · The piano speaks without barlines
sections.mNote: Little runs, grace notes and pauses in the treble

sections.label: A′ · The hymn returns
sections.mNote: The last chords descend and slow into G major

cues.title: A hymn after bedtime
cues.text: Both hands begin with quiet G-major chords, like a small choir. The inner notes move with their own careful steps. Schumann lets the phrase swell a little, then closes it before beginning again.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 20, opening systems: common time, G major, piano and hairpins in chordal writing. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Speech without barlines
cues.text: The piano leaves the hymn behind. Little runs and grace notes wander through the treble, pausing under fermatas. Schumann removes the barlines: the phrase can hesitate, collect itself and begin another thought.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 20, third system: unbarred recitative, triplet groups, grace notes, pianissimo and fermatas.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The hymn finds its way back
cues.text: The opening chords return in G major. This time the ending takes longer: the chords sink, the ritardando stretches over the final bars, and the bass reaches a low G. The last sound is held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 20, final two systems: return of the opening, extended ritardando and final G-major chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The hymn begins to hesitate
transitions.how: The G-major hymn opens into separate descending lines. The bass moves beneath held upper notes; a ritardando and fermatas interrupt the regular four-beat bars. The pianist has to wait before each continuation.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 20, second system: piano descending figures, ritardando and fermatas.

transitions.title: A pause opens the recitative
transitions.to: C · The piano speaks without barlines
transitions.how: The descending bass reaches a fermata and stops. Above the silence, the right hand begins small triplet figures marked pianissimo. The barlines disappear; grace notes and chromatic turns carry the passage up into the treble.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 20, beginning of the unbarred third system.

transitions.title: The choir returns to G major
transitions.from: C · The piano speaks without barlines
transitions.how: The free piano line descends through chromatic notes and slows with a ritardando. At the double bar the G-major hymn returns, marked piano. Both hands recover their measured chords, and the four-beat bars begin again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 20, end of the unbarred passage and start of the fourth system.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The sources do not say which printed edition Donald Betts played from. Schumann’s Kinderszenen exist in a pre-publication printing, the 1839 first edition and its revised second issue, and Clara Schumann’s later edition; the recording is not matched to any of them here.

composer.epithet: A bookseller’s son who put lovers, masks and arguments into piano music, and made criticism a form of friendship.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The books offered twins, disguises, conversations that wandered away from their subject and returned by an unexpected door. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The music changes partners every few bars.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828, moved to Heidelberg the following year, and finally persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil who had much to catch up on. By 1832, paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and began building a life at the writing desk.
